meta.title: U.S. Army / DoD munitions sites tracker
meta.timezone_note: Dates and 'last checked' values are recorded in America/Phoenix (UTC-7) calendar dates unless a source gives another zone.
meta.inclusion_rule: Includes every clearly named military/DoD facility on EPA's current OB/OD list as of the March 11, 2025 table (page also marked July 14, 2026), plus JMC conventional demil hubs named in the Oct 1, 2025 Hrycak briefing when they map to those facilities, plus Camp Minden, Savanna Army Depot, and Lake City Army Ammunition Plant. Commercial explosives plants, DOE sites, NASA Wallops, and the Saipan DFEMS entry on the same EPA list are omitted from this draft pending a later decision.
meta.coordinate_policy: Latitude and longitude are EPA FRS LATITUDE83/LONGITUDE83 for the site's RCRA ID when available. Collection method and accuracy are recorded when FRS provides them. Coordinates are not guessed or manually offset.
meta.verification_policy: verified: the listed facts were confirmed from official or other allowed primary sources. partly verified: official identity (and usually the EPA listing or a documented incident) is confirmed, but inventory, current operations, or some incident details remain incomplete. unverified: a claim was recorded but not confirmed against a primary source. Blank fields mean no source, not a zero or a no.
meta.source_exclusions: This draft does not cite NYT, CNN, MSNBC/MS NOW, Fox News, Snopes, or PolitiFact.

sites.name: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
sites.known_energetics: Bulk lead azide stored wetted in 68 55-gallon plastic drums in two earth-covered magazines; Col. Aaron C. Teller (71st Ordnance Group EOD) states the total weight is 9,773.5 lb. The plant also has a conventional munitions load-assemble-pack mission. This draft does not inventory other energetics on site.
sites.current_status: As of Nov 23, 2026 (America/Phoenix): the planned in-place detonation had not occurred. The original date was Nov 20; the Army postponed to Nov 23, then announced Nov 25. The Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay of EPA's emergency treatment permit on Nov 19, pending a ruling on the emergency stay motion in No. 26-3374; as of a CourtListener docket review on Nov 23, that merits ruling had not issued. Iowa Public Radio reported that President Trump posted on Truth Social on Nov 23 that he ordered the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit agrees they can go forward, and subject to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. IAAAP also holds a regular RCRA OB/OD permit (EPA ID IA7213820445) listed as permitted through Sept 28, 2028. The emergency permit for in-place magazine detonation is a separate authorization, issued Nov 13, 2026, effective through Feb 11, 2027.

notable_incidents.summary: Army plan to destroy 68 drums of crystallized, unserviceable lead azide by controlled in-place detonation in two earth-covered magazines. EPA issued an emergency RCRA permit on Nov 13, 2026. The shot did not take place on Nov 20 or Nov 23, 2026, and remained subject to a court stay and a reported presidential stand-down order.

sites.notes: The closest documented historical analog for bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums is Savanna Army Depot (1984). A March 21, 2014 Army article attributed DoD's 2004 green-primaries work to concern over a 40-year-old deteriorating lead azide stockpile at IAAAP. A separate research log kept with this draft has the claim-by-claim review.

sites.name: Savanna Army Depot Activity
sites.coordinate_method: GDT-ADDRESS MATCHING (GEOCODING); reference: entrance point of a facility or station. FRS also lists a SEMS point at 42.21, -90.313331; this draft uses the RCRA record and does not average the two.
sites.permit_status: Not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list
sites.known_energetics: William Shaneyfelt, safety officer at Savanna Army Depot Activity, described Vietnam-era surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums in a 1984 paper to the DoD Explosives Safety Board. Electrolysis destroyed about half the stockpile; the remainder was repacked. The public record reviewed for this draft does not establish what happened to the remaining drums after 1984.
sites.current_status: A former Army depot. EPA FRS lists BRAC and SEMS interests under ID IL3210020803. It is not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list. Present land use and whether any energetic material remains were not independently confirmed in this draft.

notable_incidents.summary: Shaneyfelt paper (21st Explosives Safety Seminar, Houston, Aug 28–30, 1984): surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating drums; sale attempts failed; electrolytic destruction halted after about half the stockpile; remaining leaking drums were repacked. The paper also describes a process-building contamination accident in which sodium azide washdown reacted with brass/copper debris and caused a 'loud, though not extremely dangerous, explosion.' That event was not a storage-drum detonation.

sites.notes: Closest documented historical analog to IAAAP's bulk lead azide drums. Post-1984 fate of the remaining material is a research gap.

sites.name: Camp Minden (former Louisiana Army Ammunition Plant)
sites.epa_name: STATE OF LOUISIANA MILITARY DEPT - CAMP MINDEN / U.S. ARMY LOUISIANA ARMY AMMUNITION PLANT
sites.branch: Louisiana Military Department (Army National Guard installation; former Army ammunition plant)
sites.epa_id_notes: FRS also lists RCRA IDs LAR000009662, LA0213820533, and LAR000037267 for Camp Minden / Louisiana Army Ammunition Plant records.
sites.coordinate_source: EPA FRS RCRAINFO LA0213820533 (NAD83). Chosen over the Camp Minden address-matched point because FRS records interpolation-map with a 30-meter accuracy value.
sites.coordinate_method: INTERPOLATION-MAP; accuracy_value=30; reference: point where substance is released
sites.permit_status: Not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list
sites.known_energetics: M6 propellant and clean-burning igniter (CBI) left from Explo Systems contractor storage of Army-origin material. EPA approved contained-burn destruction of about 16 million pounds of M6 and CBI in June 2016. These are HD 1.3 propellant/igniter materials, not primary explosives such as lead azide.
sites.current_status: The 2012–2016 emergency disposal campaign used a contained-burn chamber after open burning was dropped following public opposition. This draft has not independently confirmed current residual holdings, if any, after that campaign.

notable_incidents.summary: Explosion of a magazine at Explo Systems, Camp Minden. EPA chronology: Louisiana State Police later identified about 10 million pounds of unsecured M6; the town of Doyline (about 400 homes) was evacuated during operational hours.

Army Explosives Safety Board report cited in the EPA chronology: the probability of an explosives event related to long-term storage of M6 at Camp Minden was 'likely'; the Board recommended open burn/open detonation within two years.
EPA approved a contained-burn system after tests showed 99.99% destruction of chemicals of concern, for about 16 million pounds of M6 and CBI.

About 120,960 pounds of CBI auto-ignited in an earth-covered magazine and destroyed the bunker. Louisiana National Guard reported no injuries. An Army Explosive Safety Technical Assistance Visit then advised that remaining CBI was too dangerous to handle and should be destroyed in place, with some magazines remotely ignited because entering them was not acceptable.

sites.notes: Closest recent official parallel to IAAAP's 'cannot safely move it, destroy in place' finding, though the chemistry differs.

This draft did not independently retrieve the full AP article body (Cloudflare block during collection).

sites.notes: Local outlets also covered the 2018 fire and later reported that one of the injured workers, Andrew Goad, died of his injuries. That fatality was not independently confirmed from AP in this pass.
